title: Sis Ganj and Rakab Ganj
hookLine: where Guru Tegh Bahadur was killed and where his body was cremated

lines: CAR HORNS, CARTS, A SWEET SHOP.
cards: Car horns. A man pushing a cart stacked with sacks. A wedding-card shop, a sweet shop, a rickshaw wedged sideways in the lane.

Old Delhi's great market street, Chandni Chowk, is loud from morning to night. And right in the middle of it, between the stalls, a gurdwara with a white front and a gold dome, its singing drifting out into the traffic.
Across the city stands a second gurdwara tied to the same day. Two buildings, one death. Today, why it takes two.

teach.h: SIS GANJ: WHERE HE GAVE HIS HEAD.
teach.b: First, Sis Ganj. Sis is the Punjabi word for head.
Year one told the story: Guru Tegh Bahadur, the ninth Guru, would not give up his faith, nor let others be forced from theirs, and he was beheaded in the open square of Chandni Chowk.
Gurdwara Sis Ganj stands at that spot, right in the market, and tradition says it keeps the trunk of the tree under which he was killed. Second, Rakab Ganj.
This path has met both carriers: Bhai Jaita, who took the head north to Anandpur, and Lakhi Shah Vanjara, who took the body home and set his own house alight.

teach.h: RAKAB GANJ: WHERE THE HOUSE BURNED.
teach.b: Tradition says Gurdwara Rakab Ganj stands where that house burned.
Third, why two. Danger split the Guru's body two ways, and the panth would not lose either.

It marked the place of the death and the place of the fire, and kept walking to both: one in the loud middle of a market, open to anyone between errands, the other marking a fire lit in secret by a man with a cart.

Fourth, a line from the Guru's own saloks near the end of the Granth, in paraphrase: whatever has come into being will pass away, today or tomorrow; so sing the praises of the Lord, and let the other tangles go.
He wrote about the body passing. Then his own body passed, and two ordinary men made sure it was honored.

how: Sikhs visiting Delhi go to Gurdwara Sis Ganj in Chandni Chowk and Gurdwara Rakab Ganj, and both are crowded on the day Guru Tegh Bahadur's martyrdom is remembered.

games.q: what does “sis ganj and rakab ganj” mean?
o: two busy Delhi markets that the Guru's followers once ran
two forts outside Delhi that the ninth Guru once held
two Delhi gurdwaras: where he died and where he was cremated

games.q: Sis Ganj and Rakab Ganj: tap the pairs.

s: the Guru's head and body were honored in the same place
the head went to Anandpur with Bhai Jaita; the body was cremated where Rakab Ganj now stands.
Sis Ganj stands in the middle of a busy market
it's in Chandni Chowk, among the shops.
tradition says a trader, Lakhi Shah Vanjara, burned his own house to cremate him in secret.

games.q: a friend in Delhi has time for one stop and wants to stand where Guru Tegh Bahadur gave his head. where do you send them?
o: Rakab Ganj, where the house burned.
Sis Ganj, in the middle of Chandni Chowk.
games.why: Sis Ganj stands where he was beheaded, among the market stalls. Rakab Ganj marks the cremation.

practice: Hear the horns, the carts, the shopkeepers calling, and let the noise be there.
Then walk, in your mind, through the open doors of Sis Ganj and let the noise fall behind you, standing quietly where the market once watched a man refuse to be moved.
Step back out into the street carrying a little of that quiet, and if you pray, rest on Waheguru.

wordCard.voice: Sis Ganj and Rakab Ganj. Two gurdwaras in Delhi: one where Guru Tegh Bahadur was beheaded, one where his body was secretly cremated. Today's word.

orig.note: sis (ਸੀਸ) is the Punjabi word for head; the gurdwara marks where Guru Tegh Bahadur was beheaded.

carryVoice: Your line: where he gave his head. He stood firm for other people's freedom as well as his own. Go gently.
